content: The case against the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China (commonly known as the Alliance) for alleged incitement to subvert state power has reached its verdict on Friday, August 21, following a 24-day trial. Li Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung, who pleaded not guilty, finally heard the ruling. Former Alliance vice-chair Chow Hang-tung represented herself as a barrister in the case. While in prison, she had no computer or internet access, and wrote hundreds of pages of submissions by hand. At her application, the court played in full the two years of candlelight vigils for the June 4 incident, recreating the lights in Victoria Park, along with testimony from eyewitnesses of the crackdown. "So I am the last defendant, and also the last vice-chair of the Alliance, which is the first defendant in this case... I am now 41 years old, a barrister, and there's not much else to my simple background." Chow said with a smile as she began. Over six days of testimony, she smiled from time to time, but also broke down in tears several times. What do the June 4 vigils and the slogan "End one-party dictatorship" mean to Chow Hang-tung? What was her "intent"? This podcast episode continues to take readers into the courtroom, recreating through voice performance Chow's testimony and the cross-examinations by the judge and prosecution. Replay: Voice performance — Li Cheuk-yan's testimony: I have no hatred in my heart, only love. Related reports on the Alliance case.
